title: Gibbs Phenomenon
body:
Near a jump discontinuity, the partial sums of a [[Fourier Series]] **overshoot the jump by about
9% of its height, and adding more terms does not fix it**. The ripple gets narrower and moves
closer to the jump, but the peak height converges to $\approx 1.089$ times the jump rather than to
the jump.

The reason: convergence of the series at a jump is *pointwise*, not *uniform*. Every individual
point eventually converges (to the midpoint of the two one-sided limits, see
[[Periodic Function]]), but the worst error over the whole interval does not shrink to zero. Smooth
sinusoids cannot reproduce a vertical edge, and the [[Fourier Coefficients]] of a discontinuous
function decay only like $1/n$, which is too slow.

It is visible in practice: ringing artefacts around sharp edges in JPEG images and in filtered
audio are this, since compression truncates the series. [[Image Processing]] in
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] hits the same effect from the other direction.
